notes.meaning: Peter introduces himself as both a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ. He writes to believers who have received the same precious gift of faith that the apostles possess. This faith is given through the righteousness of Jesus Christ, who is our God and Savior.

Peter prays that grace and peace will increase abundantly in the lives of his readers. Grace is God's unearned favor, and peace is the calm rest of being reconciled to Him. These blessings multiply as believers grow in their personal knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.

God uses His own divine power to give believers everything they need for spiritual life and godliness. These gifts are not earned by human wisdom, but come through knowing Christ, who called us by His own glory and goodness. Because Christ provides all that is required, believers have full spiritual resources from the very start of their new life.

God has given believers great and precious promises so they can escape the sinful rot of the world. By trusting these promises, Christians come to share in God's holy character and live out His likeness. This divine work frees believers from the control of evil desires and helps them walk in pure, spiritual life.

differ.view: Emphasizes that sharing the divine nature means the restored image of God in holiness and righteousness, rather than becoming divine in essence.
Teaches that believers partake of God's holy character and spiritual life, but humans can never share God's essential divine being.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Sees this verse as a central foundation for the doctrine of theosis, where believers are transformed to share in God's divine life and energies by grace.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Understands partaking in the divine nature as receiving a share in God's life through sanctifying grace, while remaining entirely finite human creatures.

notes.meaning: Because God has given such great blessings, believers must put forth real effort to grow. Faith is the starting point, but Christians are called to supply moral courage to their faith. With that courage, they must also add spiritual knowledge, which gives wisdom for daily choices.

To knowledge, believers are told to add self-control, keeping their impulses and passions under proper limits. Next comes perseverance, which means patiently enduring hardships without grumbling against God. On top of perseverance, they must add godliness, living with deep reverence and heartfelt love toward God.

Believers must build on godliness by showing brotherly kindness, treating fellow Christians with warmth and family affection. Finally, they are to crown all these virtues with selfless love toward everyone. This love reaches beyond the church community to care for all people, even enemies.

When these holy traits exist and keep growing in a Christian, they keep that person active and fruitful. A true knowledge of Jesus Christ is not meant to sit idle in the mind. Instead, it moves believers to do practical good and show real evidence of their faith.

Anyone who misses out on these virtues is spiritually blind and cannot see distant, heavenly realities. Such people only pay attention to temporary things right in front of them. Worst of all, they have forgotten the wonderful mercy of having their past sins washed away by Christ.

Peter urges his readers to be eager and diligent to make their calling and election sure. Practicing these Christian virtues gives visible evidence of God's work in a person's life. Walking steadily in these habits keeps a believer from stumbling into spiritual disaster.

differ.view: Teaches that God's election is eternal and unconditional, so diligence in holy living does not secure election before God, but confirms assurance in the believer's conscience.
Teaches that election is conditional upon continuing faith and obedience, warning that believers who fail to add these virtues can stumble and lose their salvation.
Holds that salvation is permanently secure, so making election sure means cultivating good works to establish personal confidence and visible proof of one's calling.

notes.meaning: Those who grow in these godly virtues will receive a rich and joyful welcome into heaven. Their entrance into the eternal kingdom of Jesus Christ will be full of honor and triumph. God generously rewards the faithful obedience and perseverance of His people.

Peter explains that he will keep reminding his readers of these truths, even though they already know them and stand firm. People are naturally forgetful, and spiritual dangers are always present. Repeating foundational truths helps protect believers from being led astray by false teaching.

Peter views his earthly body as a temporary tent where his soul lives for a brief time. As long as he remains in this life, he considers it his solemn duty to stir up the minds of his readers. Frequent reminders keep the hearts of believers awake and responsive to God.

Peter knows that he will soon lay aside his earthly tent in death, just as Jesus had foretold. Years before, the Lord had indicated that Peter would suffer a martyr's death in his old age. Knowing that his life on earth was ending made Peter even more eager to serve the church while he still could.

The apostle promises to do everything he can to ensure that his readers will recall these truths after he is gone. By writing these letters, he leaves behind a lasting guide for the church. A faithful minister cares deeply that God's people remain rooted in truth long after his death.

The message of the gospel is not made of clever, made-up myths like those found in pagan religion. Peter and the other apostles personally saw the majesty and glory of Jesus with their own eyes. Their testimony about the power and coming of the Lord is based on solid, firsthand historical fact.

Jesus received divine honor and glory from God the Father during the Transfiguration. The magnificent presence of God spoke from heaven, declaring that Jesus is His beloved Son in whom He is fully pleased. This heavenly voice confirmed that Jesus is the true, promised Messiah sent to save the world.

Peter, James, and John personally heard this voice from heaven while they were with Jesus on the holy mountain. The mountain was called holy because God revealed His glorious presence there in a special way. This breathtaking event gave the apostles undeniable proof of Christ's divine dignity.

Believers also have the Old Testament prophecies, which are completely reliable and confirmed by Jesus. Peter compares the prophetic Scriptures to a lamp that provides necessary light in a dark room until the morning arrives. Christians should pay close attention to God's word until the day of Christ's return dawns in fullness.

Above all, readers must realize that no prophecy in Scripture ever came from a prophet's own personal ideas or imagination. The prophets were not making clever guesses about what might happen in the future. Everything recorded in the prophetic word comes from a source far higher than human insight.

Biblical prophecy was never produced simply by the will or choice of human beings. Instead, holy men spoke messages from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. Because God's Spirit guided their words, Scripture is fully inspired and can be completely trusted.
